Outcome: Depressive symptoms (lower is better)

## Study A
Found: benefit
Claim: Higher serum vitamin D was associated with a lower probability of depression in all cohorts of adults aged 20-44.
Sentence: "The estimates for the log vitamin D slope parameter were negative for all cohorts; as vitamin D increased, the probability of having no depression increased, while the probability of depression decreased."
Measured as: depressive symptoms (depression outcome categories)
Population: Adults aged 20-44 from NHANES 2007-2018: pregnant women, postpartum women, non-pregnant/non-postpartum women, and men
Intervention: Serum vitamin D concentration (observational exposure)
Comparator: Lower serum vitamin D concentration
Design: cross-sectional study
Sample size: not reported
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

## Study B
Found: no effect
Claim: Vitamin D levels were significantly associated with postpartum depressive symptom scores (EPDS); direction not stated in the abstract.
Sentence: "Significant associations were identified between EPDS scores and the levels of estrogen, progesterone, thyroid hormones (TSH, FT3, and FT4), inflammatory markers (CRP and ferritin), vitamin D, and coagulation parameters (APTT and INR)."
Measured as: postpartum depressive symptoms (EPDS)
Population: 860 postpartum women recruited at hospital discharge (1-2 weeks after childbirth) at a tertiary hospital in Timisoara, Romania
Intervention: Blood vitamin D level (measured, not given)
Comparator: Across participants by vitamin D level
Design: cross-sectional study
Sample size: 860
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported
